(Current assets - inventory) : current liabilities, written as x : 1.
The ability of a business to pay its short-term debts as they fall due.
Expanding revenue faster than the business can finance, so that cash runs out while inventory and receivables grow.
Actions near the year end that make the statement of financial position look better than the position through the year, for example paying creditors from cash.

front: Effect of paying a payable when the current ratio is above 1
back: Both totals fall by the same amount, so the current ratio rises (the acid test ratio rises only if it is above 1).

front: Is a high current ratio always good?
back: No. It may mean idle cash, slow-moving inventory or receivables not collected. Compare with the industry and earlier years.
Collect receivables faster, hold less inventory, raise long-term finance, sell surplus assets. Each has a cost.
A profitable business can run out of cash if inventory and receivables grow faster than cash comes in.
